title: What Is a Polymer?
description: Long chains of repeating units — and why size changes everything

concepts.title: Monomers and Polymers
concepts.contentHtml:
A polymer is a long molecule made of repeating monomer units linked end-to-end. Polyethylene is thousands of -CH₂- units; DNA is a polymer of nucleotides; proteins are polymers of amino acids.

The number of repeating units (the degree of polymerization) ranges from a few hundred (industrial polymers) to billions (DNA in some cells).

Polymers can be linear, branched, or cross-linked into a network. Each topology gives different mechanical and chemical properties.

concepts.title: Why Long Molecules Are Different
concepts.contentHtml:
Compared to small molecules, polymers have fundamentally different physics. They entangle — chains tangle around each other, giving viscoelastic flow.

They have a glass transition temperature T_g, below which the chains can't move and the material is hard and brittle, above which it's soft and rubbery. Polystyrene is glassy at room temperature; rubber bands are above T_g.

And they're rarely fully crystalline: many freeze into tangled glasses, and even 'crystalline' ones like polyethylene are semicrystalline, with ordered regions separated by tangled amorphous ones.

concepts.title: Natural vs Synthetic
concepts.contentHtml:
Nature was making polymers long before Staudinger formalized the concept in the 1920s. Cellulose, lignin, silk, rubber, DNA, proteins — all polymers, all evolved.

Synthetic polymers (Bakelite 1907, polyethylene 1933, nylon 1935) transformed materials in the 20th century. Annual global production now exceeds 400 million tonnes, more by volume than steel.

The boundary blurs: bioplastics use bio-derived monomers; engineered proteins are designed polymers. Nature and industry are converging.

concepts.title: Addition Polymerization
concepts.contentHtml:
Addition polymerization works on monomers with a C=C double bond. A free radical, cation, or anion attacks the double bond, opens it, and chains start growing — each new monomer adding to the active end.

Polyethylene from ethylene (CH₂=CH₂), polystyrene from styrene, PVC from vinyl chloride. Initiator + heat or pressure starts the chain; termination happens when two active ends combine or disproportionate.

concepts.title: Condensation Polymerization
concepts.contentHtml:
Condensation polymerization joins monomers by eliminating a small molecule (water, methanol, HCl). Each step loses a leaving group.

Polyester (from a diol + dicarboxylic acid), polyamides like Nylon (from a diamine + diacid). Each junction is an ester or amide bond.

Step-growth has an interesting kinetic: high molecular weights are reached only at very high conversion (>99%). Tiny amounts of monofunctional impurity cap chains and ruin properties.

concepts.title: Living Polymerization
concepts.contentHtml:
In living polymerization, chains grow without any termination step — they remain active until you add more monomer or shut them off deliberately.

This gives narrow molecular weight distributions and lets you build block copolymers (poly-A then switch monomers, get poly-A-block-poly-B).

Anionic, ATRP (atom transfer radical polymerization), and RAFT polymerizations have made precise polymer architectures routine — a far cry from the broad distributions of the early 20th century.

title: Properties of Polymeric Materials
description: From rubber bands to bullet-proof vests

concepts.title: Thermoplastics vs Thermosets vs Elastomers
concepts.contentHtml:
Thermoplastics melt and reflow on heating (PET, polyethylene, polystyrene). They can be recycled (in principle).

Thermosets form irreversible cross-linked networks during curing — bakelite, epoxy resins. They can't be re-melted.

Elastomers are lightly cross-linked rubbers — natural rubber, silicones — that recover after large deformations. Cross-link density tunes the modulus.

concepts.title: Strength and Toughness
concepts.contentHtml:
High modulus comes from rigid backbones and oriented chains. Aramid fibers (Kevlar) have an extended hydrogen-bonded sheet structure — five times stronger than steel by weight, but only along the fiber direction.

Engineering polymers (polycarbonate, ABS) balance strength, toughness, and processability. Drawing a polymer fiber aligns chains and dramatically increases its tensile strength.

concepts.title: Functional Polymers
concepts.contentHtml:
Conducting polymers (polyacetylene, PEDOT) earned the 2000 Nobel — they conduct electricity through doped π-conjugated backbones.

Smart polymers respond to stimuli: shape-memory polymers remember a programmed shape; pH-responsive polymers swell or collapse; temperature-responsive polymers (poly-NIPAM) precipitate above a critical temperature.

Biodegradable polymers (PLA, PHB) decompose into small, harmless molecules — a major direction for reducing plastic waste.

concepts.title: Proteins
concepts.contentHtml:
Proteins are linear polymers of 20 different amino acids linked by peptide bonds. The sequence determines a unique 3D fold (mostly) — shaped by hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic packing, electrostatics, and disulfide bridges.

The folded structure determines function. Catalytic proteins are enzymes; structural proteins like collagen and keratin build tissue; transport proteins like hemoglobin carry oxygen.

Misfolding causes disease — Alzheimer's (amyloid), prion diseases. Sickle cell anemia is a related case: a mutant hemoglobin that clumps into fibres. The 'protein folding problem' (predicting structure from sequence) was largely solved by AlphaFold in 2020 — a deep-learning revolution.

concepts.title: Nucleic Acids
concepts.contentHtml:
DNA is a double-stranded polymer of four bases (A, T, G, C) on a sugar-phosphate backbone. Base pairing (A-T, G-C) gives the famous double helix.

RNA is similar but single-stranded, with U replacing T. mRNA carries protein-coding sequences from DNA to ribosomes; tRNA reads codons; rRNA forms the ribosome itself.

The sequence-specific information storage of nucleic acids is the basis of all biology — and increasingly of nanotechnology, where DNA origami builds structures by sequence-programmed self-assembly.

concepts.title: Polysaccharides
concepts.contentHtml:
Sugars polymerize via glycosidic bonds. Cellulose (β-1,4 glucose) is the structural component of plants — the most abundant organic polymer on Earth.

Starch (α-1,4 glucose) is plants' energy storage. The α vs β linkage difference makes one digestible by us and the other not.

Glycogen, chitin (in insect shells and fungal walls), pectin, hyaluronic acid — polysaccharides build tissues, store energy, and lubricate joints across all life.

title: Plastic Pollution & the Future
description: Living with the materials we created

concepts.title: The Plastic Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
The world produces ~400 million tonnes of plastic per year. Recycling rates are below 10%. Most ends up in landfills, incinerators, or the environment.

Polyethylene and PET take centuries to degrade in soil. Microplastics (sub-mm fragments) are now found in oceans, soils, food, and human blood.

The chemistry that made plastic so useful — durability, chemical inertness — is exactly what makes the waste problem hard. Designing for end-of-life from the start is the new frontier.

concepts.title: Chemical Recycling
concepts.contentHtml:
Mechanical recycling (melt and remold) degrades polymers each cycle. Chemical recycling breaks polymers back to monomers, which can be re-polymerized to virgin-quality material.

Glycolysis or methanolysis depolymerize PET. Pyrolysis cracks polyolefins into fuels or chemical feedstocks. Enzymatic recycling (PETase) is a biological route.

Scaling chemical recycling economically — competing with cheap virgin polymers from petrochemicals — is the challenge.

concepts.title: Bio-based and Self-Healing
concepts.contentHtml:
Bioplastics (PLA from corn, PHA from bacteria) replace petroleum feedstocks. Some are also biodegradable — a double win.

Self-healing polymers contain reversible bonds (Diels-Alder, hydrogen bonds, ionic) that re-form after damage. Imagine plastic auto bodies that heal scratches in sunlight.

Vitrimer materials behave like thermosets at room temperature but reflow and reshape on heating — combining strength and recyclability. Polymer chemistry continues to invent answers to challenges the previous generation of polymers created.
